findings.title: Task rows still open long after the 60-minute takeover rule
findings.why_it_matters: §0.4 lets a claim be taken over when it is more than 60 minutes old with no commits, but these rows are still published as 'in progress' or 'queued' hours later. A new session reading the board cannot tell whether the work is live, abandoned or already done elsewhere, which is how the same task ends up executed twice.

findings.title: Duplicate section numbers
findings.why_it_matters: Two pairs of section numbers are reused (§4 and §43), so a citation such as 'see §43' is ambiguous and an append-only log can silently overwrite a neighbour's record during a rebase. The brief's coordination protocol depends on section numbers being unique.

findings.title: Section numbers out of ascending order
findings.why_it_matters: Section numbers decrease partway through the file (a lower number appended after a higher one), which breaks the append-only ordering convention in §0 and makes 'the latest record' hard to locate by number alone.

findings.title: Task ids claimed on more than one row
findings.why_it_matters: Two sessions holding the same task id is the collision the brief's claim protocol exists to prevent; the rows survive side by side, so the board no longer says who owns the work.
findings.recheck: grep -n '^| T' COORDINATION.md | awk -F'|' '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -d

findings.title: Very large single HTML pages on GitHub Pages
findings.why_it_matters: A page above a few hundred kilobytes is slow on mobile and expensive to re-verify by hand. These are generated from row-level ledgers, so the payload grows with every pass instead of being paginated or split per sport.
findings.recheck: git ls-files '*.html' | xargs ls -l | sort -k5 -n | tail -8

findings.title: Placeholder wording left in published pages
findings.why_it_matters: Placeholder text in a published research page reads as an unverified claim.

findings.title: Files named 'evidence' hold network-attempt logs, not verified values
findings.why_it_matters: The directory name invites a reader to treat these files as proof of a fixture or a price. They record the official URLs a previous session tried plus the transport outcome, so they are useful for discovery and for reproducing a read, but no value in them is verification. The desk published here uses them only to find official URLs and re-reads every value itself.

evidence.quote: 35 attempt logs; keys seen: complete, excerpt_policy, final_url, http_status, id, method, notes, observations, observed_after, observed_before, raw_response_sha256, role, scope, sha256, sport, url; 12 of the first 12 carry no response payload

findings.title: Session record without a section number
findings.why_it_matters: Every other session record is numbered, so an unnumbered record cannot be cited in a task row or a handoff note and is invisible to number-based collision checks.

findings.title: Gaps in the section numbering sequence
findings.why_it_matters: Numbers §20, §21, §22, §23, §24, §33, §36, §37, §54, §55 are never used. That is not corruption - renumbering after collisions leaves holes - but it means a reader cannot infer how many sessions have reported from the last number, which is exactly the ambiguity that caused the T55 collision.
